title: Topic modelling reveals rapid but uneven growth in marine structure-from-motion photogrammetry research
content:
Abstract
Photogrammetry has emerged as an important tool within marine biology and ecology, enabling researchers to map and monitor marine habitats, assess biodiversity, and study ecological processes in three dimensions. To complement previous reviews and elucidate current trends within this rapidly developing field, we conducted a systematic review of SfM photogrammetry in marine biology and ecology, analysing 466 studies published between 1973 and 2022 using a topic modelling approach. We identify the dominant research themes driving strong growth in the use of SfM photogrammetry in the published literature, particularly exploring exponential growth observed since 2015. We identified 10 distinct topics and grouped these into broader themes: including methodological refinement, habitat mapping, conservation and management, and assessing change. Key findings include a shift in emphasis over time. Early work focussed on study design and technological development and as the field developed research turned towards advancing analytical techniques, reflecting growing methodological sophistication while also highlighting persistent technical constraints. Coral reef studies were a dominant theme, consistent with previous reviews and reflecting the ecological significance and vulnerability of these ecosystems, as well as the characteristics that make them well suited to photogrammetry. Remote sensing was a frequently co-occurring topic, emphasizing its role in connecting multiple areas of marine research. In contrast, marine mammal studies demonstrated high specificity, highlighting the distinct challenges and opportunities associated with studying megafauna using photogrammetric approaches. The topic model revealed uneven integration among research themes, with some topics functioning as connectors and others forming more specialized subfields. Despite advances in many areas, important knowledge gaps are also highlighted, particularly regarding the integration of emerging technologies such as machine learning, AI-assisted annotation and learned-reconstruction methods with SfM workflows. Future research should explore these intersections to enhance data analysis capabilities, improve ecological interpretation, and test the applicability of SfM photogrammetry across a wider range of marine environments.
